column1: # title: ENG-205 Beowulf Part 2 — 4 Main Ideas
# topic: Beowulf Part 2 (Another Attack to Another Celebration at Heorot)
What happens in the section Another Attack
column2: While the Danes slept after the feast, Grendel's mother broke into Heorot, seized Aeschere, took back "Grendel's bloodied hand," and fled to the fen (around line 1251).

column1: Why Beowulf is absent during the attack
column2: Beowulf was elsewhere, because after the treasure-giving he had been given "another lodging" (around line 1300).

column1: How Grendel's mother compares to Grendel
column2: The poet says her onslaught was less than Grendel's only as an "Amazon warrior's" is less than an "armored man's" (around line 1283).

column1: Why Grendel's mother flees so quickly
column2: The "hell-dam was in panic, desperate to get out" once the warriors grabbed their swords, so she snatched one man and fled (around line 1292).
Hrothgar answers Beowulf with "Rest? What is rest? Sorrow has returned," and mourns Aeschere as his dearest friend (around line 1322).

column1: Why Hrothgar says Grendel's mother attacked
column2: Hrothgar says Grendel's mother "has taken up the feud" because Beowulf killed Grendel, and she is "driven to avenge her kinsman's death" (around line 1333).

Hrothgar describes a mere above which a "frost-stiffened wood" stands, where "the water burns" at night, the bottom "has never been sounded," and a hunted hart will die rather than dive in (around line 1360).

column1: Beowulf's two-part reply to Hrothgar's grief
column2: Beowulf answers Hrothgar, who is mourning Aeschere, that "it is always better to avenge dear ones than to indulge in mourning" and that each man should "win glory before death" (around line 1385).

Hrothgar and Beowulf followed Grendel's mother's tracks over cliffs and narrow paths to a "dismal wood" above "bloodshot water," where they found Aeschere's head at the foot of the cliff (around line 1421).
When a war-horn stirred the sea-dragons and serpents, Beowulf shot one with an arrow and the men dragged it ashore with "barbed boar-spears" (around line 1432).

column1: How Beowulf arms himself for the mere
column2: Beowulf put on his "fine-webbed mail" and gold helmet "adorned with boar-shapes" and took Hrunting, the sword Unferth lent him (around line 1445).

Beowulf asks Hrothgar to "act like a father" to him, take care of his young comrades, send his treasures to Hygelac, and give Unferth his own sword, then vows "With Hrunting I shall gain glory or die" (around line 1475).
The "wolfish swimmer," Grendel's mother, carried Beowulf to her underwater "court," a "hellish turn-hole" lit by firelight, while sea-beasts tore at his chain-mail (around line 1506).
Beowulf found "his battle-torch extinguished" because "the shining blade refused to bite," the first time the heirloom failed (around line 1523).
Beowulf "flung his sword away" to "rely on the might of his arm," because a man seeking "enduring glory" must not count the cost of his life (around line 1531).

column1: How the mail shirt saves Beowulf
column2: When Grendel's mother pinned Beowulf and drew "a broad, whetted knife," his chain-mail turned the blade, and "Holy God decided the victory" (around line 1546).
Beowulf seized "an ancient heirloom from the days of the giants," a sword "so huge and heavy" only he could wield, and it severed her neck bone (around line 1557).
The blade "began to wilt into gory icicles" and melted "as ice melts," because the blood of the "poisonous fiend" was so scalding (around line 1607).

column1: What Beowulf brings back from the mere
column2: Beowulf saw "treasure in abundance" but carried back only Grendel's head and "the inlaid hilt embossed with jewels" (around line 1614).

column1: What happens in the section Another Celebration at Heorot
column2: Grendel's head was "hauled by the hair" across the drinking floor, Beowulf told of the fight, and Hrothgar's hall feasted again (around line 1647).
Beowulf credits God for showing him the giant sword and pledges that Hrothgar "can sleep secure" in Heorot with his troops (around line 1672).
The gold hilt handed to Hrothgar is engraved with how "war first came into the world" and how "the flood destroyed the tribe of giants," with runes naming whom it was made for (around line 1688).

column1: Why Hrothgar tells the story of Heremod
column2: Hrothgar warns that Heremod "killed his own comrades," "grew bloodthirsty," and "gave no more rings," the kind of king Beowulf must not become (around line 1710).
Hrothgar urges "O flower of warriors, beware of that trap," telling Beowulf to "choose... the better part, eternal rewards" and warning "Do not give way to pride" (around line 1758).

column1: The arrow image in the sermon
column2: Hrothgar describes pride entering a man while "the soul's guard, its sentry, drowses," until a demon "archer" shoots him in the heart and he "bestows no gold" (around line 1744).
Hrothgar lists the ends that await Beowulf as "illness or the sword," "a sudden fire or surge of water," a "jabbing blade or javelin from the air," or "repellent age" (around line 1763).

column1: The gifts and exchanges in Part 2, in order
column2: Hrothgar first promises "coffers of coiled gold," Unferth lends Hrunting, Beowulf gives Hrothgar Grendel's head and the gold hilt, Hrothgar promises treasure "tomorrow morning," Beowulf returns Hrunting, and Hrothgar gives twelve treasures.
Beowulf had Hrunting brought to Unferth, called it "a friend in battle," and "put no blame on the blade's cutting edge" (around line 1807).
Beowulf promises to bring a "hedge of spears" if Denmark is threatened and says Hrothgar's son Hrethric will find many friends among the Geats (around line 1836).
Hrothgar says the Geats could find no man "worthier of acclaim as their king" than Beowulf if Hygelac dies (around line 1850).

column1: How Beowulf has united two peoples
column2: Hrothgar says Beowulf has drawn the Geats and Danes into "shared peace and a pact of friendship" despite past hatreds, so gifts will cross "the gannet's bath" (around line 1857).
Hrothgar kissed Beowulf and wept, troubled by "two forebodings," the stronger being that they would never meet "face to face" again (around line 1873).
As Beowulf leaves, the narrator foretells that Hrothgar was "a peerless king until old age sapped his strength" (around line 1885).
Hrunting fails and the giant sword melts, which suggests that Beowulf's victories depend on his own strength and God's help rather than on weapons.

column1: Grendel's mother as the cycle of war
column2: Grendel's mother stands for the recurring cycle of war, because her revenge for Grendel provokes Beowulf's revenge for Aeschere in turn.
The joyful feast gives way to the night attack, and then "a light appeared" in her hall as Grendel's mother died, followed by a new feast in Heorot.
Old Hrothgar, who has "wintered into wisdom," warns young Beowulf that his strength will fade, which sets up the old king Beowulf will become.
